journeys.name: The wanderings and homecoming of Odysseus

legs.note: Sacking the Cicones' city on leaving Troy.
Storm rounding Cape Malea drives the fleet off its course home.
Wind and current sweep the ships past Cythera.
Nine days adrift before making the Lotus-eaters' shore.
On to the land of the lawless Cyclopes.
Aeolus's floating island, keeper of the winds.
Six days' sailing (ἑξῆμαρ, Od. 10.80), landfall at Telepylus on the seventh (ἑβδομάτῃ, 10.81).
The sole surviving ship reaches Circe's island.

Circe sends Odysseus across Ocean to the Cimmerians' sunless land for the nekyia. Homer gives no real-world geography for this stop (mythical tier; no coordinates in this gazetteer, so the leg cannot be drawn on a real map).
Return from the house of Hades to Aeaea, per Circe's own instruction (12.1-2). Same honesty caveat as the outbound leg: the Cimmerian land itself carries no coordinates.
Circe's sailing directions: the Sirens first.
Past the Sirens toward the strait; Scylla's rock on one side.
Charybdis on the other side of the same strait; Circe advises hugging Scylla's side to avoid Charybdis wholesale, so the two are effectively one strait-transit.
On to the island of the Sun's cattle.

The wrecked, sole-surviving Odysseus drifts nine days after Charybdis re-swallows the wreck near Thrinacia and washes up on Ogygia, Calypso's island (12.447-450). Ogygia carries no coordinates in this gazetteer (Homer's own geography puts it at the 'navel of the sea', far from any coast); the leg is recorded for narrative completeness but cannot be drawn on a real map.

After seven years with Calypso and Hermes's intervention, the raft voyage of seventeen/eighteen days ends in sight of the Phaeacians' land. Origin has no fixed position; the map renders the departure as a faded stub resuming at Scheria.

The Phaeacian ship, sailing overnight, sets the sleeping Odysseus and his gifts ashore at the Cave of the Nymphs in Ithaca -- the nostos's endpoint (John's explicit call: this line must end at Ithaca).
Homebound from Troy, the fleet reaches Sounion, where Apollo strikes down the helmsman Phrontis at the tiller; Menelaus puts in to bury him, delaying the voyage.
Resuming the voyage, the fleet is rounding the height of Malea when Zeus sends the storm that will scatter it.

Zeus splits the fleet at Malea: part of it (not Menelaus's own ship) is driven onto Crete, wrecking near the cliff by Gortyn on the south coast, at the border of Phaestus -- a specific landfall distinct from Knossos (the only Crete pin in this gazetteer). The men escape the wreck (3.297-298); the ships do not. Recorded for completeness as part of Menelaus's fleet's fate, not his own itinerary.
The other five dark-prowed ships -- Menelaus's own among them, since he goes on to wander Egypt/Cyprus/Phoenicia (4.81-85) -- are driven on by wind and current to Egypt (3.299-300), bypassing Crete.
Becalmed off the Nile mouth, the fleet's course takes it to the island of Pharos, a day's sail offshore.
Menelaus returns from Pharos to Egypt's river, offers full hecatombs, and raises a cenotaph for Agamemnon (Od. 4.581–584).
The gods grant a fair wind and send him swiftly home (Od. 4.585–586); the voyage itself is not separately narrated.

Named in Menelaus's summary of his eight years' wandering (4.81-85); the list gives no order or itinerary logic connecting its members, so this leg records only that Cyprus was visited, not when or from where.

Phoenicia/Sidon, from the same summary list (4.83-84); order relative to the other list-members is not given by the poem. (Menelaus's Sidonian guest-gift, a silver krater, is separately mentioned at 4.615-619 and 15.115-119, without narrating a visit there.)

The Ethiopians, from the summary list (4.84); Homer's Ethiopians are a legendary people 'sundered in two' at the ends of the earth (Od. 1.22-24) -- not a real-world itinerary stop, no coordinates in this gazetteer. The poem lists this people among Menelaus's wanderings without giving any sequence (Od. 4.83–85).

The Erembi, from the same list-line as the Sidonians (4.84); their identity is a genuinely unresolved ancient crux (Strabo 1.2.34: Poseidonius argues for the Arabians, others for the Troglodytae) -- no consensus site exists to pin, ancient or modern. The poem lists this people among Menelaus's wanderings without giving any sequence (Od. 4.83–85).
Libya, from the summary list (4.85), described in almost fairy-tale terms (triple-lambing flocks); order relative to the other list-members is not given by the poem.
Nestor's contingent, sailing with Odysseus's, makes the first stop at Tenedos to sacrifice -- before the quarrel among the Achaean leaders splits the returning fleets.
Nestor's own ships, now sailing with Diomedes's and (soon) Menelaus's, press on and are overtaken by Menelaus at Lesbos, debating the safer route north or south of Chios.
On a god-sent omen they strike out on the open-sea crossing to Euboea, making harbor at Geraistos by night.
From Geraistos -- where Diomedes's squadron peels off for Argos (3.180-182) -- Nestor's own ships run on before a steady wind straight to Pylos.

journeys.name: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Sparta, and back

legs.note: Telemachus and the Ithacan crew sail all night (2.434) and reach Pylos at dawn, as the Pylians are sacrificing on the shore (3.4-5).
By chariot with Peisistratus, reaching Diocles' house at Pherae by nightfall of the first day.
A second day's driving across the wheat-plain brings them to Sparta and Menelaus's palace.

The return voyage, engineered by Athena's warning to avoid the suitors' ambush (15.27-42). The ambush itself is set at the island Asteris, explicitly named, 'between Ithaca and rugged Same' (4.844-847, echoed 15.29). But the escape route Homer actually narrates (15.295-300) runs past real Elean landmarks -- Crounoi, the stream Chalcis, Pheae, Elis -- then simply 'the swift islands' (θοῇσιν νήσοισιν, 15.299), unnamed in the received text; whether these are Asteris and its neighbors or an unrelated group is a genuine crux, not resolved by the poem's own wording. Flagged here, not resolved.
